title: The invisible gorilla
hookLine: in a study by Simons and Chabris, viewers counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit

cards: Count the passes. That's the whole job. On a short video, a few people in white shirts and a few in black weave around each other, bouncing basketballs.

Watch only the white team and count its passes. You keep a careful tally. Partway through, a person in a full gorilla suit walks into the middle of the game, stops, faces the camera, thumps their chest, and walks off.
Afterward the researchers ask one question: did you notice anything unusual? Close to half the people who watched said no.

teach.b: The psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris ran this study, in a paper titled Gorillas in Our Midst.
The name for what happened is inattentional blindness: when attention is fully on one task, something plainly in view can go unseen. Viewers didn't report seeing it and then forgetting.
As far as they could tell, it was never there. They weren't careless. They did exactly what they were asked, and did it well.

teach.h: FOCUS HIDES WHAT IT ISN'T ON.
teach.b: The focus that made them good counters is the same focus that hid the gorilla. Attention works like a flashlight: what it lights gets sharper, and everything outside the beam goes darker.
You can't have the beam without the dark. The second lesson is quieter.
From the inside, missing something doesn't feel like missing anything. Nobody felt a gap; the scene seemed complete. That's why the blind spot is so easy to live in.

A person can count passes all day, at work, at home, in a marriage, and walk past something that matters, standing in the middle of the room thumping its chest. So the question from this lab isn't how do I see everything.
It's humbler: what am I missing? Asked now and then, it widens the beam just enough.

how: Researchers study inattentional blindness by giving people a demanding task, such as counting passes, and asking afterward whether they noticed an unexpected event that happened in plain view.

o: an animal symbol for strength in old stories
something in plain view that goes unseen while you focus
a hidden danger only experts know to look for

games.q: you're counting passes carefully, and a gorilla walks through the middle of the game. what happens for close to half the viewers?
o: they keep counting and never see it.
games.why: they never see it. the focus that made them good counters hid the gorilla.

practice: Without moving much, let your eyes find three things in the room you hadn't noticed before: a color, a shadow, a sound under the other sounds.
Then close your eyes, bring to mind one person you see often, and ask gently what you've been missing about them while you count your passes, holding the question open without forcing an answer.

wordCard.voice: The invisible gorilla. Something plainly in view that goes unseen, because attention is busy somewhere else. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what am I missing. A humbler question than how to see everything. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Simons, D. J., and Chabris, C. F., Gorillas in our midst: sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events, Perception 28 (1999)
